detailedAnswer: JDK contains JRE, JRE contains JVM. Source compiles to bytecode with javac; the JVM loads, verifies, and executes bytecode, with JIT compilation for hot code. Portability comes from bytecode plus a platform-specific JVM. Remember: JDK is for development (compiler, tools), JRE is for running (libraries + JVM), JVM is the runtime engine itself. Class loading, bytecode verification, and the runtime memory areas (heap, stack, metaspace) are the usual follow-up topics.
question: Module 0 revision: JDK, JRE, JVM in one minute
shortAnswer: JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM; source → bytecode → JVM execution → JIT for hot code.
tips: If asked 'is Java fully platform independent?', answer: bytecode is portable, but the JVM itself is platform-specific.
title: Revision: JVM basics

detailedAnswer: Encapsulation: bundle data with the methods that use it and expose it only through controlled access (private fields, public methods). Abstraction: expose what an object does, not how (abstract classes and interfaces). Inheritance: a subclass reuses and extends a superclass — favour composition over inheritance when reuse is not truly an is-a relationship. Polymorphism: the same call behaves differently by runtime type — method overriding (runtime) versus overloading (compile time). In an interview, always give a concrete example: e.g. a Payment interface with CardPayment and UpiPayment implementations, chosen at runtime.
question: Module 0 revision: OOP in one minute
shortAnswer: Encapsulation hides state, abstraction hides complexity, inheritance reuses behaviour, polymorphism lets one interface take many forms.
tips: Name all four pillars, then immediately give one real example — interviewers remember examples, not definitions alone.
title: Revision: OOP principles

commonMistakes: Comparing strings with == instead of equals().
Concatenating inside a loop instead of using StringBuilder.
detailedAnswer: String is immutable: every concatenation creates a new object, so building strings in a loop with + is slow — use StringBuilder (single-threaded) or StringBuffer (synchronized). Literals are interned in the string pool, so "abc" == "abc" can be true, but never rely on it: compare content with equals(), and use equalsIgnoreCase() or Objects.equals() when nulls are possible. String is final, so it cannot be subclassed, which also makes it safe as a HashMap key. Know the common traps: String.split takes a regex, substring and trim return new strings, and string comparison with == is the classic interview bug.
question: Module 0 revision: Strings in one minute
shortAnswer: String is immutable and pooled; use StringBuilder for loops, equals() for content, == only for reference identity.
title: Revision: Strings

detailedAnswer: List allows duplicates and is ordered; Set forbids duplicates; Map stores key-value pairs with unique keys. ArrayList gives fast random access; LinkedList is better for frequent inserts/removes in the middle but slow for random access. HashMap gives fast key lookup but no ordering guarantee — use LinkedHashMap for insertion order, TreeMap for sorted keys. HashSet is backed by a HashMap; TreeSet keeps elements sorted. ConcurrentHashMap is the thread-safe map choice, with no null keys or values, unlike HashMap (one null key, many null values) and Hashtable (synchronized, no nulls). Always state time complexity: ArrayList get is O(1), HashMap get/put is O(1) on average.
question: Module 0 revision: Collections in one minute
shortAnswer: List: ordered + duplicates. Set: unique. Map: key-value. ArrayList for access, HashMap for lookup, ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps.
tips: When asked 'which collection?', answer with the access pattern first: ordered? unique? keyed? thread-safe? — then name the class.
title: Revision: Collections

commonMistakes: Empty catch blocks.
Catching Exception before its subclasses, which does not compile.
Using exceptions for normal control flow.
detailedAnswer: Throwable splits into Error (serious JVM problems, do not catch) and Exception. Checked exceptions (e.g. IOException) must be caught or declared with throws; unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and subclasses, e.g. NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException) need not be declared. Use try-with-resources for anything AutoCloseable so resources close even on failure. Catch the most specific exception first — a broad catch of Exception hides bugs. Never swallow an exception with an empty catch block: log it or rethrow it, possibly wrapped. In Spring apps, prefer translating checked exceptions into meaningful runtime exceptions at service boundaries and handling them centrally with @ControllerAdvice.
question: Module 0 revision: Exceptions in one minute
shortAnswer: Checked exceptions must be handled or declared; unchecked (RuntimeException) need not be. Catch specific exceptions, use try-with-resources, never swallow exceptions.
title: Revision: Exceptions

detailedAnswer: Generics let you write one class or method that works for many types while the compiler checks types for you — List<String> cannot accidentally hold an Integer. Because of type erasure, generic type information is removed at compile time: you cannot do new T(), check instanceof List<String>, or overload foo(List<String>) and foo(List<Integer>) together. Wildcards: <? extends T> is a producer (you read from it, PECS), <? super T> is a consumer (you write into it). Bounded type parameters (<T extends Comparable<T>>) restrict what a type argument may be. Generics do not work with primitives — use wrapper classes and autoboxing, and be aware of the small boxing cost in hot loops.
question: Module 0 revision: Generics in one minute
shortAnswer: Generics give compile-time type safety; type erasure means generic types do not exist at runtime. PECS: producer extends, consumer super.
tips: PECS is the single most-asked generics point: say it, then give an example (copying from List<? extends Number> into List<? super Number>).
title: Revision: Generics

commonMistakes: Reusing a stream after a terminal operation.
Using forEach to mutate shared state inside a parallel stream.
detailedAnswer: A stream pipeline has a source (collection, array, generator), zero or more intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap, sorted, distinct — lazy, return a stream), and exactly one terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce, count, anyMatch — triggers execution). Streams do not modify the source and are single-use: reuse throws IllegalStateException. Intermediate operations are lazy, so filter().map() does nothing until a terminal operation runs, which enables short-circuiting with findFirst() or limit(). A lambda is shorthand for an anonymous implementation of a functional interface (one abstract method), e.g. (a, b) -> a + b for a Comparator. Method references (String::toUpperCase, System.out::println) are lambdas in shorter form. Parallel streams split work across threads, but only help for large, CPU-bound, stateless pipelines — never use them with shared mutable state.
question: Module 0 revision: Streams in one minute
shortAnswer: Streams are lazy pipelines: source → intermediate operations → one terminal operation. Lambdas are concise implementations of functional interfaces.
title: Revision: Streams and lambdas

detailedAnswer: Optional is a container that is either empty or holds one non-null value: use Optional.ofNullable(value), map/flatMap to transform, orElse/orElseGet for a fallback, and orElseThrow for a meaningful exception. Prefer orElseGet over orElse when the fallback is expensive, because orElse evaluates eagerly. Never call get() without checking, never use Optional as a method parameter or a field in an entity, and never return null where you promised an Optional. The built-in functional interfaces: Predicate<T> (test, returns boolean), Function<T,R> (apply), Consumer<T> (accept, no result), Supplier<T> (get, no input), plus BiFunction, BiPredicate, and primitive versions like IntPredicate and ToIntFunction that avoid boxing. Custom functional interfaces need exactly one abstract method and are usually marked @FunctionalInterface.
question: Module 0 revision: Optional and functional interfaces in one minute
shortAnswer: Optional models 'value may be absent' explicitly. Core functional interfaces: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier, plus Bi- variants and primitive specializations.
tips: If asked why not just return null: Optional forces the caller to handle absence at compile time instead of discovering a NullPointerException at runtime.
title: Revision: Optional and functional interfaces

commonMistakes: Creating unbounded threads instead of using a pool.
Assuming volatile makes compound actions atomic.
Forgetting to shut down an ExecutorService.
detailedAnswer: Each thread has its own stack; all threads share the heap, which is why unsynchronized access to shared mutable state causes race conditions. synchronized and ReentrantLock provide mutual exclusion; volatile guarantees visibility of a variable's latest value but not atomicity (volatile++ is still a race). Prefer the java.util.concurrent toolkit: ExecutorService and thread pools instead of new Thread(), ConcurrentHashMap and CopyOnWriteArrayList instead of synchronized wrappers, CountDownLatch and CyclicBarrier for coordination, and CompletableFuture for async pipelines. Know the deadlock ingredients (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) and how to avoid them: acquire locks in a fixed order, use timeouts (tryLock), and keep critical sections small. Always shut down an ExecutorService, or the JVM will not exit.
question: Module 0 revision: Concurrency in one minute
shortAnswer: Threads share heap memory; synchronize access to shared mutable state, prefer java.util.concurrent utilities over raw wait/notify, and use ExecutorService instead of creating threads by hand.
title: Revision: Concurrency basics

detailedAnswer: Without synchronization, one thread's write to a shared variable may never become visible to another thread, and the JVM or CPU may reorder operations. The Java Memory Model fixes this with happens-before relationships: a write happens-before a later read if they are ordered by a rule such as: unlocking a monitor happens-before locking the same monitor; a write to a volatile variable happens-before a later read of that volatile; starting a thread happens-before its first action; and a thread's last action happens-before another thread's join() on it. Practical consequences: publish shared state safely (final fields, volatile, or proper synchronization), do not rely on Thread.sleep() for visibility, and remember that 64-bit long/double reads and writes are atomic only if the field is volatile. Double-checked locking is correct only with a volatile instance field.
question: Module 0 revision: Java Memory Model in one minute
shortAnswer: The JMM defines when one thread's writes become visible to another. Happens-before rules — volatile, synchronized, thread start/join, final fields — are what guarantee visibility and ordering.
tips: Frame every JMM answer around one phrase: 'happens-before guarantees visibility and ordering; without it, there is no guarantee at all.'
title: Revision: Java Memory Model

detailedAnswer: Objects start in Eden (young generation); survivors move to survivor spaces and, after enough collections, are promoted to the old generation. Minor GC cleans the young generation and is frequent but cheap; major/full GC cleans the old generation and is rarer but costlier. Modern collectors: G1 (the default since Java 9, region-based, balances latency and throughput), ZGC and Shenandoah (very low pause times, good for large heaps). Reachability, not reference counting, decides liveness — even cyclic references are collected if unreachable. Practical points: avoid finalize() (deprecated, unpredictable), do not call System.gc() in production code, watch for memory leaks via static collections or unclosed listeners/caches holding references, and choose a collector by measuring pause time and throughput, not by reputation.
question: Module 0 revision: Garbage collection in one minute
shortAnswer: The GC reclaims unreachable objects. Most objects die young, so the heap is generational: young generation collected often, old generation rarely. Tune the collector to the app's latency or throughput goal.
tips: If asked 'how would you investigate high GC pauses?', answer: GC logs, heap dump analysis, and checking for allocation hotspots — in that order.
title: Revision: Garbage collection

commonMistakes: Deserializing untrusted input.
Forgetting serialVersionUID and then breaking compatibility on a class change.
Serializing fields that should be transient (passwords, caches).
detailedAnswer: Reflection (Class, Method, Field) lets code inspect types, create instances, and call methods whose names are only known at runtime — frameworks like Spring and Jackson rely on it. Costs: slower than direct calls, breaks encapsulation (setAccessible), and defeats compile-time checking, so prefer it in framework code, not business logic. Serialization (java.io.Serializable) writes an object's state to a stream and reads it back; transient fields are skipped, static fields are not serialized, and serialVersionUID controls version compatibility — change the class without updating it and deserialization fails. Security warning: never deserialize untrusted data with native Java serialization; prefer JSON (Jackson) for data exchange. For deep copies, serialization works but is slow — consider a copy constructor or a mapping library instead.
question: Module 0 revision: Reflection and serialization in one minute
shortAnswer: Reflection inspects and invokes classes at runtime; serialization converts an object graph to bytes and back. Both are powerful and both bypass normal compile-time safety — use them deliberately.
title: Revision: Reflection and serialization

detailedAnswer: The flow is: DriverManager (or a DataSource) gives a Connection, you create a Statement or PreparedStatement, execute a query, and read the ResultSet. Always prefer PreparedStatement over Statement: parameters are bound safely, which prevents SQL injection and lets the database reuse execution plans. Close Connection, Statement, and ResultSet in reverse order — try-with-resources does this for you. Handle SQLException (checked) by translating it into a meaningful application exception and rolling back the transaction where needed. In real applications, never open a raw connection per request: use a connection pool such as HikariCP (Spring Boot's default) and let Spring's JdbcTemplate or Spring Data JPA handle the boilerplate. Know the transaction basics: auto-commit off, commit on success, rollback on failure.
question: Module 0 revision: JDBC in one minute
shortAnswer: JDBC is Java's API for relational databases: load a driver, get a Connection, use PreparedStatement for parameterized SQL, close everything with try-with-resources, and pool connections in production.
tips: The one JDBC answer interviewers always want: PreparedStatement prevents SQL injection; Statement with string concatenation does not.
title: Revision: JDBC

detailedAnswer: SOLID: S — a class has one reason to change; O — open for extension, closed for modification (extend via new code, not edits); L — a subclass must be usable wherever its superclass is expected; I — many small interfaces beat one fat interface; D — depend on abstractions, not concretions (this is what Spring DI implements). Patterns to name with an example each: Singleton (one instance — use an enum or Spring's singleton scope, not a hand-rolled double-checked lock unless asked); Factory (create objects without exposing construction logic); Builder (readable construction of objects with many optional fields); Strategy (swap algorithms at runtime, e.g. payment methods); Observer (notify subscribers of state changes); Decorator (add behaviour without subclassing); Adapter (make incompatible interfaces work together); Repository (abstract data access behind an interface). Never recite patterns without an example — one real use case each is what scores.
question: Module 0 revision: Design patterns and SOLID in one minute
shortAnswer: SOLID: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion. Patterns to know cold: Singleton, Factory, Builder, Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Adapter, Repository.
tips: When asked for a pattern, name it, state the problem it solves, then give a one-line example from a real codebase.
title: Revision: Design patterns and SOLID

detailedAnswer: Inversion of Control flips responsibility: instead of a class creating its own dependencies with new, the Spring container instantiates beans and injects their dependencies. Dependency injection comes in three forms — constructor injection (preferred: dependencies are final, the object is never half-built, and testing is easy), setter injection, and field injection (avoid: hidden dependencies, hard to test). Stereotype annotations mark beans for component scanning: @Component (general), @Service (business logic), @Repository (data access, also translates persistence exceptions), @Controller/@RestController (web layer). @Bean methods in a @Configuration class define beans explicitly, e.g. third-party classes you cannot annotate. Bean scopes: singleton (default, one per container), prototype (new instance per request), plus request/session scopes in web apps. Lifecycle hooks: @PostConstruct for setup after injection, @PreDestroy for cleanup.
question: Module 0 revision: Spring IoC in one minute
shortAnswer: IoC means the container creates and wires beans instead of your code doing it. Inject via constructor (preferred), declare beans with @Component/@Service/@Repository or @Bean, and let Spring manage their lifecycle.
tips: If asked 'why constructor injection?', the answer is three words: immutability, testability, fail-fast — missing dependencies fail at startup, not at runtime.
title: Revision: Spring IoC and dependency injection

detailedAnswer: @SpringBootApplication is three annotations in one: @Configuration (this class defines beans), @EnableAutoConfiguration (let Boot configure beans for you), and @ComponentScan (find your @Component classes). Auto-configuration classes, listed in Spring Boot's auto-configuration imports, create beans only when conditions hold — @ConditionalOnClass (a library is present), @ConditionalOnMissingBean (you have not defined your own), @ConditionalOnProperty (a property is set). That is why adding spring-boot-starter-web gives you an embedded Tomcat and a DispatcherServlet with no XML, and why defining your own DataSource bean replaces Boot's default. Configuration comes from application.properties or application.yml, bound to type-safe classes with @ConfigurationProperties, and overridden per environment with Spring profiles (@Profile, spring.profiles.active). Debug with --debug or the conditions report to see which auto-configurations matched and why others did not.
question: Module 0 revision: Spring Boot auto-configuration in one minute
shortAnswer: @SpringBootApplication bundles @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan. Auto-configuration supplies beans conditionally, based on what is on the classpath and what you have already defined.
tips: The killer interview line: auto-configuration backs off when you define your own bean — @ConditionalOnMissingBean is the mechanism.
title: Revision: Spring Boot auto-configuration

commonMistakes: Putting business logic in controllers.
Returning 200 for everything, including errors.
Using GET with a body or POST for pure reads.
detailedAnswer: The DispatcherServlet is the front controller: it receives every request, consults handler mappings to find the matching @Controller method, resolves arguments (@PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody), and writes the response via message converters (JSON with Jackson by default). @RestController is @Controller + @ResponseBody — it returns data, not views. REST conventions: GET for reads (200), POST for creation (201 with a Location header), PUT for full replacement, PATCH for partial updates, DELETE for removal (204), and 404 for missing resources, 400 for invalid input, 401/403 for auth problems. Validate request bodies with Bean Validation (@Valid, @NotNull, @Size) and return field errors cleanly. Centralize error handling with @ControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler so controllers stay focused on happy paths. Keep controllers thin: they translate HTTP to service calls and back, and all business logic lives in services.
question: Module 0 revision: Spring MVC and REST in one minute
shortAnswer: DispatcherServlet routes requests to @RestController methods. Use @GetMapping/@PostMapping with proper status codes, validate input, and handle errors centrally with @ControllerAdvice.
title: Revision: Spring MVC and REST

detailedAnswer: Define an interface extending JpaRepository<Entity, Id> and Spring Data generates the implementation at runtime: save, findById, findAll, delete, plus derived queries parsed from method names (findByEmailAndActiveTrue). For anything the naming rules cannot express, write @Query with JPQL or a native query. Entities map tables with @Entity, @Id, @GeneratedValue, and relationships @OneToMany/@ManyToOne — fetch type matters: LAZY loads associations on access, EAGER loads them immediately, and lazy access outside a transaction throws LazyInitializationException. The N+1 problem (one query for parents, then one per child) is fixed with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection. Transactions belong on service methods with @Transactional (rollback by default only for unchecked exceptions), and read-only transactions (readOnly = true) are a cheap optimization for queries.
question: Module 0 revision: Spring Data JPA in one minute
shortAnswer: Spring Data JPA generates repository implementations from interfaces: derived query methods, @Query for custom JPQL, and @Transactional boundaries on services — with lazy loading and the N+1 problem as the classic traps.
tips: When asked about N+1, name the symptom (many small queries), the cause (lazy loading in a loop), and the fix (JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph) — all three in one breath.
title: Revision: Spring Data JPA in one minute

commonMistakes: Storing secrets or passwords in a JWT payload.
Accepting tokens without verifying signature or expiry.
Storing passwords in plain text or with a fast hash like MD5.
detailedAnswer: Authentication (who are you?) happens first, via login credentials, OAuth2, or a token; authorization (what may you do?) follows, via roles or authorities (ROLE_USER, ROLE_ADMIN). In Spring Security, a filter chain intercepts requests, an AuthenticationManager verifies credentials, and a SecurityContext holds the authenticated principal for the request. A JWT has three Base64URL parts: header (algorithm), payload (claims such as sub, roles, exp), and signature (HMAC or RSA over header + payload). The server verifies the signature with its secret or public key and rejects expired tokens — the payload is readable by anyone, so never put secrets in it. Access tokens are short-lived; refresh tokens (stored securely, ideally httpOnly) issue new ones. Stateless JWT auth scales because no server-side session is needed, but tokens cannot be revoked before expiry without a denylist — keep lifetimes short. Always serve auth over HTTPS, store passwords hashed with BCrypt (never plain or MD5), and protect against CSRF where cookies carry auth.
question: Module 0 revision: Security and JWT in one minute
shortAnswer: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. JWT is a signed, stateless token: header.payload.signature — verify the signature and expiry, never trust the payload alone.
title: Revision: Security and JWT

detailedAnswer: A microservice owns one bounded context and its own database — no shared tables across services, or you have a distributed monolith, not microservices. Services communicate synchronously (REST, gRPC) or asynchronously (events via Kafka/RabbitMQ); async messaging decouples services but introduces eventual consistency, so design for it (idempotent consumers, outbox pattern for reliable publishing). Cross-cutting concerns: an API gateway for routing and auth, service discovery for locating instances, centralized configuration, distributed tracing (trace IDs across calls), and resilience patterns — timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers. Spring Boot Actuator adds production endpoints: /actuator/health (liveness and readiness), /actuator/metrics (JVM, HTTP, custom counters via Micrometer), /actuator/info, and /actuator/env. Expose health publicly if needed, but restrict metrics and env behind authentication — they leak internals. Pair Actuator with Prometheus/Grafana for metrics and a log aggregator for logs.
question: Module 0 revision: Microservices and Actuator in one minute
shortAnswer: Microservices split a system into independently deployable services, each owning its data. Actuator exposes health, metrics, and info endpoints so you can observe them — but expose only what is safe.
tips: If asked 'monolith or microservices?', answer with trade-offs: microservices buy independent scaling and deployment but cost operational complexity — do not present them as always better.
title: Revision: Microservices and Actuator

detailedAnswer: Records (Java 16) are concise immutable data carriers: record Point(int x, int y) {} generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString — use them for DTOs and value objects, not for mutable entities. Sealed classes (Java 17) restrict which classes may extend them (permits), making hierarchies exhaustive for switch expressions. Pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16) removes casts: if (obj instanceof String s) { use s directly }. Switch expressions (Java 14) return values and support arrow syntax, and pattern matching for switch (Java 21) matches on types and guards. Text blocks (Java 15) write multiline strings with """ without escaping every quote — ideal for SQL and JSON samples. var (Java 10) infers local variable types but is not dynamic typing and cannot be used for fields or method signatures. Virtual threads (Java 21) make blocking-style code scale to millions of threads, but do not fix shared-state bugs — synchronization rules still apply.
question: Module 0 revision: Modern Java features in one minute
shortAnswer: Records for data carriers, sealed classes for closed hierarchies, pattern matching for instanceof and switch, text blocks for multiline strings, and var for local type inference.
tips: Name the Java version for each feature — interviewers use version numbers to check whether knowledge is current.
title: Revision: Modern Java features
Revision: SQL fundamentals
question: Module 0 revision: SQL fundamentals in one minute
shortAnswer: SQL reads and changes data in relational tables: SELECT with WHERE filters rows, aggregates with GROUP BY and HAVING summarise them, and keys and constraints keep the data valid.
detailedAnswer: Start from the shape of the data: a table has columns with data types, one primary key that uniquely identifies each row, and foreign keys that link rows in one table to rows in another. Constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT) are rules the database enforces so bad data cannot be saved. The everyday statements are SELECT (read), INSERT (add), UPDATE (change), and DELETE (remove), plus CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE for the structure itself. Filter rows with WHERE before they are grouped; use aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX with GROUP BY to summarise, and HAVING to filter the grouped results — WHERE cannot do that job because it runs before grouping. Order results with ORDER BY and limit them with LIMIT (or the equivalent in your database). For dates, know the basic date and time functions of the database you use, and remember that SQL is case-insensitive for keywords but the data itself may be case-sensitive depending on collation.
followUps: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
What does a primary key guarantee that a UNIQUE constraint does not?
When would you use DELETE versus TRUNCATE?
tips: Say the order of execution out loud: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT — it explains most SQL surprises.
commonMistakes: Filtering grouped results with WHERE instead of HAVING.
Forgetting that COUNT(*) counts rows while COUNT(column) skips NULLs.

title: Revision: SQL joins, subqueries, window functions and CTEs
question: Module 0 revision: SQL joins, subqueries, window functions and CTEs in one minute
shortAnswer: Joins combine rows across tables, subqueries nest one query inside another, window functions rank or total rows without collapsing them, and CTEs name a subquery so the main query stays readable.
detailedAnswer: Joins answer 'which rows go together?': INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows on both sides, LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills in NULLs where there is no match, and a SELF JOIN joins a table to itself (for example, an employee to their manager). UNION stacks result sets vertically and removes duplicates, while UNION ALL keeps them — the two queries must return the same number and compatible types of columns. A subquery is a query inside another query, in the SELECT list, the FROM clause, or a WHERE clause with IN or EXISTS; EXISTS is usually the better choice when you only need to know whether a match exists. Window functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) compute a value per row while keeping every row — unlike GROUP BY, they do not collapse rows, which is why they are the standard way to find the top N rows per group or a running total. A CASE expression adds if-then logic inside a query, and a CTE (WITH ... AS ...) gives a subquery a name so a long query reads top to bottom instead of inside out. When a query is slow, the first things to check are a missing join condition (which explodes into a cross product) and a missing index on the join or filter columns.
followUps: How would you find the second-highest salary in each department?
When would you use a subquery instead of a join?
What is the difference between ROW_NUMBER and RANK?
tips: For 'top N per group' questions, reach for ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY value) and filter on the row number — it is the answer interviewers expect.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the ON condition on a join and getting a cartesian product.
Using UNION when UNION ALL would do, paying for a sort and de-duplication nobody asked for.

title: Revision: Data types, variables and operators
question: Module 0 revision: Data types, variables and operators in one minute
shortAnswer: Java has eight primitive types and reference types; variables hold values or references, operators compute with them, and casting converts between types — widening automatically, narrowing only with an explicit cast.
detailedAnswer: The eight primitives are byte, short, int, long, float, double, char and boolean; everything else is a reference type, including arrays and objects. Each primitive has a wrapper class (Integer, Double, Boolean and so on) used when an object is required, for example in collections, and autoboxing converts between the two automatically — but unboxing a null wrapper throws a NullPointerException, a classic interview trap. Local variables must be assigned before use, instance variables get default values (0, false, null), and final marks a variable that cannot be reassigned. Operators cover arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %), comparison, logical (&&, ||, !), and the ternary (condition ? a : b); remember that && and || short-circuit, so the right-hand side may never run. Type casting: widening (int to long, int to double) happens automatically and is safe, while narrowing (double to int, long to int) needs an explicit cast and can lose data — casting 9.9 to int gives 9, not 10. String concatenation with + converts operands to strings, so 1 + 2 + "3" is "33" while "1" + 2 + 3 is "123"; evaluation is left to right. Since Java 10, var lets the compiler infer a local variable's type, but the type is still fixed at compile time — it is not dynamic typing.
followUps: What happens when you unbox a null Integer?
Why does 1 + 2 + "3" give a different result from "1" + 2 + 3?
When is var allowed and when is it not?
tips: If asked about a tricky expression, evaluate it left to right and say each step out loud — that is how you avoid the string-concatenation trap.
commonMistakes: Unboxing a null wrapper and getting a NullPointerException.
Assuming a narrowing cast rounds instead of truncating.

title: Revision: Spring AOP
question: Module 0 revision: Spring AOP in one minute
shortAnswer: AOP moves cross-cutting concerns such as logging, transactions and security out of business code into aspects that Spring weaves around your methods.
detailedAnswer: Some behaviour cuts across many classes — logging, timing, security checks, transaction boundaries — and copying it into every method is noisy and error-prone. Aspect-Oriented Programming solves this by putting that behaviour in one place, an aspect, and letting Spring apply it where needed. The vocabulary: an aspect is the class holding the cross-cutting logic, a join point is a place it could apply (in Spring, a method execution), a pointcut is the expression selecting which methods (for example, all methods in a service package), advice is the code that runs (before, after, around, or when an exception is thrown), and the weaved result is a proxy around your bean. Spring AOP is proxy-based: it wraps your bean in a JDK dynamic proxy (when the bean implements an interface) or a CGLIB subclass proxy, and only public methods called from outside the bean go through the proxy — a method calling another method on the same object (this) bypasses the advice entirely, which is the most common AOP interview trap. @Around advice is the most powerful because it can run code before and after, change arguments, skip the call, or change the result; @Transactional itself is implemented as AOP advice. Keep aspects focused and pointcuts narrow: an over-broad pointcut advising everything is a performance and debugging headache.
followUps: Why does a method calling another method on the same bean bypass AOP advice?
What is the difference between JDK dynamic proxies and CGLIB proxies?
How is @Transactional related to AOP?
tips: The self-invocation trap is the AOP answer interviewers most want: advice only applies when a call goes through the proxy, never on this.method().
commonMistakes: Expecting advice to run on private methods or self-invocations.
Writing an over-broad pointcut that advises far more methods than intended.

title: Revision: Testing with JUnit, Mockito and MockMvc
question: Module 0 revision: Testing with JUnit, Mockito and MockMvc in one minute
shortAnswer: Unit tests check one class in isolation with JUnit assertions and Mockito stand-ins for its dependencies; MockMvc tests a controller's HTTP behaviour without starting a server.
detailedAnswer: A unit test checks one small piece of behaviour: arrange the inputs, act by calling the method, assert the outcome with JUnit 5 assertions such as assertEquals, assertThrows and assertTrue. Real dependencies make tests slow and flaky, so replace them with Mockito test doubles: @Mock creates a stand-in, @InjectMocks builds the class under test with those stand-ins injected, when(...).thenReturn(...) programs the stand-in's answer, and verify(...) checks a method was called with the expected arguments. Test the behaviour, not the implementation — a test that breaks every time you refactor the internals is a liability, not a safety net. For the web layer, MockMvc (with @WebMvcTest) sends fake HTTP requests to a controller and checks the status code, headers and JSON body without starting a server, while @SpringBootTest loads the whole application context and is reserved for integration tests that genuinely need it, ideally with Testcontainers for a real database. The test pyramid is the guiding shape: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few slow end-to-end tests. Name tests after the behaviour they check (for example, 'rejects an order with a negative quantity'), keep tests independent so they pass in any order, and never let a test depend on the current date, a random value, or an external service.
followUps: What is the difference between a mock and a stub?
When would you use @WebMvcTest instead of @SpringBootTest?
How do you test code that depends on the current time?
tips: If a test needs a real database or network, it is an integration test, not a unit test — say so, and name the right tool (Testcontainers, @DataJpaTest) for it.
commonMistakes: Mocking the class you are actually trying to test.
Writing tests that depend on execution order or on shared mutable state.

title: Revision: SQL indexes and transactions
question: Module 0 revision: SQL indexes and transactions in one minute
shortAnswer: Indexes make lookups fast at the cost of slower writes; transactions group statements into one atomic, ACID unit, and the isolation level trades consistency against concurrency.
detailedAnswer: An index is a separate lookup structure, usually a B-tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. Index the columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY clauses, and use a composite index when queries filter on several columns together, remembering the leftmost-prefix rule: an index on (department, salary) helps queries on department alone but not on salary alone. The price is slower inserts, updates and deletes, because every index must be maintained, plus extra storage, so index deliberately and confirm with EXPLAIN rather than indexing every column. A transaction groups statements so they commit together or roll back together: BEGIN, then work, then COMMIT on success or ROLLBACK on failure. ACID sums up the guarantees: atomicity (all or nothing), consistency (rules and constraints hold after the transaction), isolation (concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work), and durability (committed data survives a crash). Isolation levels trade safety for concurrency: READ COMMITTED blocks dirty reads, REPEATABLE READ also blocks non-repeatable reads, and SERIALIZABLE blocks phantom reads too but is the slowest. Prevent lost updates, where two transactions overwrite each other, with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or optimistic locking with a version column, and keep transactions short so locks are held briefly.
followUps: When does adding an index make a query slower instead of faster?
What is the difference between READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ?
How would you prevent two users from overwriting each other's update to the same row?
tips: Answer index questions with the trade-off first: faster reads, slower writes, extra storage — then name the leftmost-prefix rule.
commonMistakes: Indexing every column and slowing down writes for no benefit.
Holding a transaction open across user input or a slow network call.

title: Revision: Transactions in Spring with @Transactional
question: Module 0 revision: @Transactional in one minute
shortAnswer: Put @Transactional on service methods: Spring wraps the method in a transaction via a proxy, rolls back on unchecked exceptions by default, and lets you control propagation and isolation.
detailedAnswer: Place @Transactional on service methods, not controllers or repositories, so one business operation maps to one transaction. It works through a proxy, which has two consequences interviewers love to test: calling another method on the same object (this) bypasses the proxy, so the transaction advice never runs, and annotating a private method has no effect because the proxy cannot intercept it. By default a transaction rolls back only on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and Error); a checked exception commits unless you set rollbackFor. Propagation controls how a method behaves when a transaction already exists: REQUIRED, the default, joins the existing transaction; REQUIRES_NEW suspends it and starts a fresh one, useful for audit logging that must survive even if the outer work rolls back; NESTED runs a savepoint inside the current transaction. Isolation picks how much concurrent interference is tolerated, matching the database levels from READ COMMITTED up to SERIALIZABLE. Mark read-only work with readOnly = true so the database and JPA can skip dirty checking and optimise the query. A classic failure is a lazy-loaded association accessed after the transaction closed, which throws LazyInitializationException: fetch what you need inside the transaction with JOIN FETCH or an entity graph instead of widening the transaction.
followUps: Why does calling a @Transactional method from another method in the same class not start a transaction?
When would you use REQUIRES_NEW instead of REQUIRED?
A checked exception was thrown but the data was still saved — why?
tips: Lead with the proxy rule: @Transactional only works when the call goes through the Spring proxy, never on self-invocation or private methods.
commonMistakes: Expecting rollback on a checked exception without rollbackFor.
Annotating private methods or relying on self-invocation to start a transaction.

title: Revision: Scheduling with @Scheduled
question: Module 0 revision: @Scheduled in one minute
shortAnswer: Enable scheduling once, then annotate methods: fixedRate runs on a fixed start-to-start interval, fixedDelay waits after the previous run finishes, and cron runs on a calendar schedule.
detailedAnswer: Add @EnableScheduling, usually on the main application class, and annotate a no-argument method with @Scheduled. fixedRate starts the next run a fixed time after the previous run started, so runs can overlap if a run takes longer than the interval. fixedDelay waits a fixed time after the previous run finished, so runs never overlap but the gap varies with how long the work takes. cron takes a six-field expression (seconds, minutes, hours, day of month, month, day of week), which is the choice for calendar schedules such as every night at 2am, and supports a zone attribute when the server timezone is not the schedule's timezone. By default Spring runs all scheduled methods on a single thread, so one slow job delays every other job: configure a TaskScheduler with a pool when jobs must run independently. Keep scheduled work idempotent, because a restart or a second instance can run it twice, and use a distributed lock or a leader election if only one instance may run it. For work that should run in the background but not on a schedule, @Async on a method (with @EnableAsync) runs it on a separate thread pool, with the same proxy rule as AOP: self-invocation bypasses it.
followUps: What is the difference between fixedRate and fixedDelay?
A scheduled job runs twice after a restart — how do you prevent that?
Why would you give the scheduler a thread pool instead of the default single thread?
tips: Say the cron field order out loud — seconds first — because getting the fields wrong is the most common scheduling mistake.
commonMistakes: Forgetting @EnableScheduling and wondering why nothing runs.
Using fixedRate for a job that must never overlap with itself.

title: Revision: Calling other services — RestTemplate vs WebClient
question: Module 0 revision: RestTemplate vs WebClient in one minute
shortAnswer: RestTemplate is the older synchronous, blocking HTTP client; WebClient is the non-blocking replacement for high-concurrency calls, and RestClient is the modern synchronous option.
detailedAnswer: When one service calls another over HTTP, RestTemplate is the classic Spring client: simple and synchronous, one thread blocked per request until the response arrives. That blocking model is fine for occasional calls but wastes threads when a service fans out to many downstream services at once. WebClient, from Spring WebFlux, is non-blocking: a small number of threads can juggle many in-flight requests, which is why it is the recommended choice for high-concurrency service-to-service calls, and it also supports streaming responses. RestTemplate is in maintenance mode, not removed, but new code should prefer WebClient for reactive stacks or RestClient, added in Spring Framework 6.1, which keeps the familiar synchronous style with a modern fluent API. Whichever client you use, create it once as a bean instead of building a new one per request, set connect and read timeouts explicitly so a slow downstream service cannot hang your threads forever, and handle error statuses deliberately rather than letting every 4xx or 5xx surface as a generic exception. For resilience, combine the client with timeouts, retries with backoff, and a circuit breaker.
followUps: When would you choose WebClient over RestTemplate?
What happens if you never set a timeout on an HTTP client?
How is RestClient different from RestTemplate?
tips: Frame the answer as a thread-economics trade-off: blocking clients hold a thread per call, non-blocking clients do not.
commonMistakes: Creating a new RestTemplate or WebClient for every request instead of reusing one bean.
Calling a downstream service with no timeout and letting threads pile up.

title: Revision: Servlet filter vs Spring interceptor
question: Module 0 revision: filter vs interceptor vs AOP in one minute
shortAnswer: Filters run at the servlet level before Spring sees the request; interceptors run inside Spring MVC around the handler method; AOP advises any Spring bean method.
detailedAnswer: A servlet filter sits in front of the DispatcherServlet and sees every request and response, but it knows nothing about Spring: it cannot tell which controller method will handle the request. Use filters for edge concerns such as logging, CORS headers, compression, or request tracing. A HandlerInterceptor runs inside Spring MVC, around the handler method, with preHandle before the controller, postHandle after it, and afterCompletion once the response is done; it knows the handler method, so it can apply logic per endpoint, for example checking a header for a specific controller or recording per-endpoint metrics. Aspect-oriented programming goes one level deeper: advice runs around any Spring bean method, not just web handlers, which is where logging, transactions and security checks on service methods belong. The request flows in this order: filter, then interceptor, then controller, then back out through interceptor and filter. CORS is typically handled at the filter level or with a global CORS configuration, not inside a controller. A common trap is doing authentication in an interceptor while expecting it to protect non-MVC endpoints such as Actuator: filters and Spring Security's filter chain cover those, interceptors do not.
followUps: Where would you add request logging: filter, interceptor, or AOP?
Why does an interceptor not protect an Actuator endpoint?
How do you apply CORS to a whole application?
tips: Draw the order in one sentence — filter, interceptor, controller — and pick the layer by asking what the code needs to know: the raw request, the handler method, or any bean method.
commonMistakes: Using an interceptor for something that must also cover non-MVC requests.
Putting business logic in a filter or interceptor instead of a service.

title: Revision: Kafka basics
question: Module 0 revision: Kafka in one minute
shortAnswer: Kafka is a distributed log: producers append events to topics split into partitions, consumers read them in order per partition, and consumer groups share the work.
detailedAnswer: A topic is a named stream of events, split into partitions so it can scale across brokers; ordering is guaranteed only within one partition, never across the whole topic. Producers append records to a topic, choosing the partition from the record key, so all events with the same key land in the same partition in order. Consumers read from partitions and track their position with offsets; a consumer group splits a topic's partitions across its members, so adding consumers scales consumption until there is one consumer per partition. Delivery is at-least-once by default: a consumer can receive the same message twice after a crash or rebalance, so consumers must be idempotent and handle duplicates gracefully. Use Kafka over synchronous REST when services should be decoupled, when many consumers need the same event, or when bursts of work should be buffered instead of overwhelming a downstream service. Compared with a traditional broker such as RabbitMQ, Kafka keeps messages durably in the log so they can be replayed, which suits event-driven systems and audit trails. The classic traps are assuming global ordering across partitions, assuming exactly-once delivery without the extra configuration and idempotent design it requires, and letting a slow consumer fall behind until the lag becomes unrecoverable.
followUps: How do you guarantee ordering for events about the same order or user?
What happens when a consumer crashes halfway through processing a message?
When would you use Kafka instead of a direct REST call?
tips: Anchor the answer on two phrases: ordering is per partition only, and delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.
commonMistakes: Assuming messages arrive in order across the whole topic.
Writing a consumer that breaks when it sees the same message twice.

title: Revision: Spring Cloud — discovery, gateway and circuit breakers
question: Module 0 revision: service discovery and resilience in one minute
shortAnswer: Services find each other through a registry instead of hardcoded URLs, traffic enters through a gateway, and circuit breakers stop calls to a failing service before it drags the rest down.
detailedAnswer: Hardcoding hostnames and ports does not survive services that scale up, move, or restart, so services register themselves with a discovery server such as Eureka, sending regular heartbeats, and look each other up by name instead of by address. Configuration is centralised in a config server so every service reads the same properties without a redeploy. All outside traffic enters through an API gateway, which routes by path, applies authentication, rate limiting and request logging in one place; the older Zuul proxy has been superseded by Spring Cloud Gateway. When a downstream service starts failing, a circuit breaker stops calling it: closed while calls succeed, open after a run of failures so calls fail fast instead of piling up threads, and half-open after a pause to try a single probe call before closing again. Hystrix, the original Netflix circuit breaker, is deprecated; Resilience4j is the current library, and it pairs with timeouts, retries with backoff, and bulkheads that limit how many threads one dependency may consume. The point of all of this is graceful degradation: a failing dependency should return a fallback or a clear error, not cascade into a system-wide outage.
followUps: Why is a hardcoded service URL a problem in a microservices system?
What are the three states of a circuit breaker?
What does a gateway do that a load balancer does not?
tips: Name the modern replacements: Spring Cloud Gateway over Zuul, Resilience4j over Hystrix — interviewers check whether the knowledge is current.
commonMistakes: Recommending Hystrix or Zuul for a new system without noting they are legacy.
Adding retries without backoff and amplifying an outage.

title: Revision: Abstract class vs interface
question: Module 0 revision: abstract class vs interface in one minute
shortAnswer: An abstract class shares code and state with its subclasses; an interface is a contract a class promises to fulfil, and a class can implement many of them.
detailedAnswer: An abstract class can hold instance fields, constructors, concrete methods and abstract methods, and it is used when subclasses share behaviour and state: a common base for payment processors that all need the same logging and validation, for example. A class extends exactly one abstract class, and the abstract class can force subclasses to implement specific methods by declaring them abstract. An interface declares a contract: method signatures, constants, and since Java 8, default and static methods, but no instance state. A class can implement many interfaces, which is how Java gets the flexibility of multiple inheritance without its ambiguity. Choose an abstract class when the types share an is-a relationship plus common implementation; choose an interface when you are describing a capability or role that unrelated classes can play, such as Comparable, Runnable, or a repository contract. Default methods let interfaces evolve without breaking existing implementations, but they blur the old sharp line, so the deciding question is still state and shared code: if subclasses need shared fields and helper methods, reach for the abstract class. A marker interface is an empty interface, such as Serializable, that simply labels a class so other code can treat it specially.
followUps: When would you pick an abstract class over an interface?
Can an interface have a method with a body?
What is a marker interface for?
tips: Answer with the decision rule, not just definitions: shared state and code means abstract class, a role many unrelated classes can play means interface.
commonMistakes: Using an abstract class where an interface would keep the design open.
Forgetting that a class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class.

title: Revision: static and final
question: Module 0 revision: static and final in one minute
shortAnswer: static means it belongs to the class, shared by all instances; final means it cannot be changed — a variable assigned once, a method never overridden, a class never extended.
detailedAnswer: A static field or method belongs to the class, not to any instance: there is one copy shared by all objects, it is accessed through the class name, and it can be used without creating an object. That is why main is static: the JVM calls it before any object exists. A static method cannot use instance fields or this, and it cannot be overridden, only hidden by a subclass method with the same signature, which is a common trap. A final variable can be assigned only once; a blank final variable, declared without a value, must be assigned in every constructor. A final method cannot be overridden, and a final class, such as String, cannot be extended at all. Final on a reference means the reference cannot be pointed at another object, but the object itself may still be mutable: a final List can still have elements added to it. Constructors cannot be final, because they are never inherited or overridden. In practice, make fields final wherever possible: it documents intent, helps the compiler and the reader, and is a building block of immutable, thread-safe objects.
followUps: Why is the main method static?
Can a final List still change?
What is a blank final variable and where must it be assigned?
tips: The two traps interviewers reuse most: final on a reference does not make the object immutable, and static methods are hidden, not overridden.
commonMistakes: Saying a final collection is immutable.
Trying to use instance fields from a static method.

title: Revision: Database migrations with Flyway
question: Module 0 revision: Flyway database migrations in one minute
shortAnswer: Flyway applies versioned SQL migration files in order and records each one, so every environment's schema evolves the same way, safely and repeatably.
detailedAnswer: Instead of editing a database by hand or letting an ORM recreate the schema, write each schema change as a versioned migration file, named by convention V1__create_orders_table.sql, V2__add_customer_index.sql, and so on. On startup Flyway checks a history table, applies any migrations that have not run yet, in version order, inside a transaction, and records them so they are never applied twice. Repeatable migrations, prefixed R__, run again whenever their checksum changes and suit views and stored procedures that are redefined rather than altered. The golden rule is never edit a migration that has already run anywhere: fix it with a new migration, because the history table's checksums would otherwise fail validation on the next deploy. Never use Hibernate's automatic schema update in production; it is a development convenience that can drop or alter columns silently. Flyway and Liquibase solve the same problem, Flyway with plain SQL files and Liquibase with database-independent change sets, and the practical choice usually comes down to team preference and whether the schema must run unchanged on several database engines.
followUps: What do you do when a migration that already ran needs a correction?
Why is automatic schema update unsafe in production?
What is the difference between a versioned and a repeatable migration?
tips: The one line interviewers want: never edit an applied migration, always add a new one.
commonMistakes: Editing an applied migration and breaking checksum validation on every other environment.
Relying on Hibernate ddl-auto in production.

title: Revision: API documentation with OpenAPI and Swagger
question: Module 0 revision: OpenAPI and Swagger in one minute
shortAnswer: OpenAPI is the standard description of a REST API; Swagger UI renders it as interactive documentation, generated from your code so it stays in step with the API.
detailedAnswer: OpenAPI is a standard, machine-readable description of an API: its endpoints, request and response shapes, parameters and status codes. Swagger UI is the web page that renders that description so a developer can read it and try calls from the browser. In Spring Boot, the springdoc-openapi library generates the description automatically from your controllers, so the documentation cannot drift far from the code the way a hand-written wiki page can. Annotations refine what is generated: @Operation describes an endpoint, @Parameter documents a query or path parameter, and @Schema describes a request or response object, including examples and which fields are required. The generated UI is typically served alongside the application during development, which makes it the first thing a new teammate or a frontend developer opens. Keep it out of public production exposure unless it sits behind authentication, since it advertises every endpoint you have. The alternative approach is contract-first: write the OpenAPI file first and generate server stubs and clients from it, which suits teams where the API contract is agreed before the code exists.
followUps: What is the difference between OpenAPI and Swagger UI?
How do you document a required field or an example response?
When would you write the OpenAPI file first instead of generating it?
tips: Stress the maintenance point: generated docs stay in step with the code, hand-written docs rot.
commonMistakes: Exposing Swagger UI publicly in production without authentication.
Documenting the API in a wiki that nobody updates after the first release.
